title: Rule-Based AI and Expert Systems 📜
intro: Before machine learning took over, AI meant writing knowledge down as rules. That approach still runs inside many systems you use. Here is how it works, and why it is still useful.

sections.heading: 1. Writing Knowledge Down

analogy.description: Every workplace has written procedures: if a customer asks for a refund within 30 days, approve it. Rule-based AI turns that kind of written knowledge into something a computer can follow.

sections.bodyMarkdown:
**Symbolic AI** represents knowledge with symbols a person can read: facts like "a penguin is a bird" and rules like "if a bird cannot fly, do not suggest flying as a way to escape". The computer combines them to reach conclusions.

How you write knowledge down matters. Simple rules work for narrow tasks. For richer subjects, people use structures that link concepts together, so the computer can follow the connections. Either way, every piece of knowledge was put there by someone, which makes the system transparent but laborious to build.

jargonBuster.simpleExplanation: AI that works with knowledge written as readable symbols, facts and rules.
The way knowledge is written down so a computer can use it.

diagram.caption: Facts plus rules give conclusions
diagram.content:
graph LR
    F["Fact: a penguin is a bird"] --> C["Combine"]
    F2["Fact: penguins cannot fly"] --> C
    R["Rule: if a bird cannot fly, it escapes on foot or by swimming"] --> C
    C --> A["Conclusion: a penguin escapes by swimming"]
diagram.alt: Two facts, a penguin is a bird and penguins cannot fly, plus a rule about birds that cannot fly, are combined to reach the conclusion that a penguin escapes by swimming.

sections.realWorld: Loan pre-checks, insurance quote forms and tax calculators all run on written rules.

sections.heading: 2. Inside an Expert System

analogy.description: A good IT helpdesk has a binder of fixes and a technician who asks questions until one fix matches. An expert system is that binder and that technician, in software.

sections.bodyMarkdown:
An **expert system** captures the know-how of specialists, such as engineers or doctors, so others can use it. It has two main parts.

The **knowledge base** stores the rules. The **inference engine** looks at the current facts, finds rules whose conditions are met and applies them. Each conclusion becomes a new fact, which may trigger further rules, until it reaches an answer.

Because every step uses a written rule, the system can always show its reasoning: "I recommended this because rules 3 and 7 applied."

jargonBuster.simpleExplanation: Software that gives specialist advice by applying rules collected from experts.
The collection of facts and rules an expert system uses.
The part that checks the facts against the rules and decides which rules apply.

diagram.caption: How an expert system reaches an answer
diagram.alt: Four steps: the user gives facts, the inference engine finds rules whose conditions are met, each conclusion is added as a new fact, and the system gives an answer with the rules it used.
steps: The user supplies the facts: "The printer is on but nothing prints."
The inference engine finds rules whose conditions are all true.
Each conclusion is added as a new fact, which may trigger more rules.
The system gives its answer and lists the rules it used.

sections.realWorld: Equipment fault-finding guides, airline crew scheduling checks and some medical triage tools use this design.

sections.heading: 3. Working Forward or Backward

analogy.description: A detective starts from the clues and sees where they lead. Someone checking a theory starts from the suspect and looks for the clues that would prove it. Expert systems can reason both ways.

sections.bodyMarkdown:
**Forward chaining** starts from the facts you have and keeps applying rules to see what follows. It suits monitoring: "the battery is low and it is night, so…".

**Backward chaining** starts from a possible answer and works back, asking only the questions needed to confirm or rule it out. It suits diagnosis: "could it be a flat battery? Then I need to know whether the lights work."

Backward chaining often asks fewer questions, because it ignores anything irrelevant to the answer it is testing.

jargonBuster.simpleExplanation: Reasoning from known facts towards whatever conclusions they lead to.
Reasoning from a possible answer back to the facts needed to confirm it.

diagram.caption: Two directions of reasoning
diagram.content:
flowchart LR
    subgraph FW ["Forward chaining"]
        F1["Facts"] --> F2["Apply rules"] --> F3["Conclusions"]
    end
    subgraph BW ["Backward chaining"]
        B1["Possible answer"] --> B2["Which facts would prove it?"] --> B3["Ask only for those"]
    end
diagram.alt: Forward chaining goes from facts, through rules, to conclusions. Backward chaining starts from a possible answer, works out which facts would prove it, and asks only for those.

sections.realWorld: A car's dashboard warning system works forward from sensor readings. A troubleshooting wizard that asks you targeted questions often works backward.

sections.heading: 4. Maps of Meaning: Ontologies and Knowledge Graphs

analogy.description: A family tree lets you work out that your mother's sister's son is your cousin, even though nobody wrote "cousin" on the chart. Linked knowledge lets computers make the same kind of deductions.

sections.bodyMarkdown:
An **ontology** is a structured description of a subject: what kinds of things exist, and how they relate. For example, a dog is a mammal, a mammal is an animal, and every animal eats.

From that, a computer can deduce that a dog eats, without anyone writing it down. Large collections of linked facts like this are called **knowledge graphs**. Search engines use them to answer questions like "how tall is the Eiffel Tower?" directly, instead of just listing pages.

jargonBuster.simpleExplanation: A structured description of the kinds of things in a subject and how they relate.
A large network of linked facts that a computer can search and reason over.

diagram.caption: A tiny ontology
diagram.content:
graph TD
    Animal["Animal: eats"] --> Mammal["Mammal"]
    Mammal --> Dog["Dog"]
    Mammal --> Cat["Cat"]
    Dog -.->|deduced| Eats["A dog eats"]
diagram.alt: Animal, which eats, has the subtype mammal, which has the subtypes dog and cat. From the links, the computer deduces that a dog eats.

sections.realWorld: The fact panel beside search results, product catalogues that group items sensibly and medical coding systems all rely on ontologies.

sections.heading: 5. Try It: Diagnose a Mars Rover

analogy.description: A rover on Mars is minutes of signal delay away from any engineer. It needs its own rule book to react in time.

sections.bodyMarkdown:
This simulation is a small expert system. Its sensors report facts: battery level, day or night, whether the solar panels are dusty, and whether the antenna is aimed at the relay satellite.

Change the facts and watch which rules fire. The rover's decision always comes from a rule you can point to, which is exactly the transparency that makes rule-based systems attractive for safety-critical work.
sections.realWorld: Spacecraft, industrial machinery and medical devices often use rule-based safety logic because every decision can be traced and checked.

interactiveWidget.title: 🚀 Try It: The Mars Rover Expert System
interactiveWidget.goal: Set the sensor facts that lead to each of the rover's decisions.
interactiveWidget.predictionPrompt: Before you change anything: which rule do you expect to fire if the battery is low at night?
hints: A rule fires only when all of its conditions are true.
Change one fact at a time and watch the rules.
interactiveWidget.successMessage: That is forward chaining: facts in, matching rules fire, a traceable decision out.
interactiveWidget.instruction: Change the sensor facts. Watch which rules fire and what the rover decides.

miniQuiz.question: What are the two main parts of an expert system?
options: A knowledge base and an inference engine
miniQuiz.praise: Correct. Rules in one part, reasoning in the other.
miniQuiz.explanation: The knowledge base stores the rules; the inference engine decides which rules apply to the current facts.

miniQuiz.question: Why are rule-based systems popular for safety-critical work?
options: Every decision can be traced to a written rule
miniQuiz.explanation: Because each decision comes from a written rule, it can be checked and explained.

miniQuiz.question: Which approach starts from a possible answer and asks only the questions needed to confirm it?
miniQuiz.praise: Right. Backward chaining works back from the answer.
miniQuiz.explanation: Backward chaining starts from a candidate answer and looks for the facts that would prove or rule it out.

teachBack.prompt: How would you explain an expert system to a colleague?
options: Software that applies experts' written rules to the facts and can show which rules it used.
Software that learns from millions of examples.
A chat assistant that knows everything.
teachBack.explanation: Exactly. Expert rules, applied to facts, with traceable reasoning.

recall.question: What makes most modern AI different from ordinary software?
recall.explanation: Most modern AI learns patterns from examples rather than only following written rules.
